title: openai/openai-agents-python v0.24.0-alpha.7 — Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.7
body:
# Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.7

## Highlights

- **Use Classic workflows alongside native execution.** Import the retained v0 runtime through `agents.classic`. This alpha also changes executor write defaults; review the upgrade actions before opening existing environments.
- **Keep conversations in your own storage.** Add durable root Sessions with `CustomStorage`, and reconcile uncertain tool effects before resuming work.
- **Add voice and hosted tools to native agents.** Connect speech workflows to a Session, or use `FileSearch`, `CodeInterpreter`, and `ImageGeneration` through compatible Responses providers.
- **Control context, completion, and usage.** Transform model input, retain selected context during compaction, review proposed answers, and limit observed root usage.

## Upgrading from 0.24.0-alpha.6

- **Review Environment write policies.** New Environments default to `write_policy="strict"`, which requires a compatible Linux or macOS executor. The working directory remains writable; use `writable_roots` for additional directories. To retain the previous remote policy, including on Windows executors, set `write_policy="legacy"` and leave `writable_roots=None`. Local execution requires strict mode. When restoring legacy remote checkpoints or profiles, select legacy explicitly; reopening does not upgrade their policy. See the [executor policy and restore rules](https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/blob/4c1190046163c09e4f67ab7254f22bea60b14894/docs/sdk/state.md#restore-executor-policy).
- **Check implicit reasoning settings.** The bundled model catalog changes the default reasoning effort from `low` to `medium` for `gpt-6-astra`, `gpt-6.1-sol`, and `gpt-5.6-sol`. Set `model_settings={"reasoning_effort": "low"}` explicitly if you need the previous effort. This describes bundled metadata; an explicit setting or provider model metadata can select another value. (#5517)
- **Rename MCP approval modes.** Replace `approval_mode="auto"` with `"native"`, and `"approve"` with `"preapproved"`. The old values are rejected; the new names preserve their respective approval behavior.
- **Update child step callbacks.** `NativeAgents.before_step` now receives one `ChildStepContext`, with `context`, `child`, and `step_index`, instead of separate child and step-index arguments. Root `before_step` callbacks keep their existing signature.
- **Handle MCP forms and URLs separately.** `ElicitationRequest` is now the union `FormRequest | UrlRequest`. Use `FormRequest.reply()` or `respond()` for forms; use `UrlRequest.reply_url_accept()` or `accept_url()` for URL consent.

## Added

- **Application-owned conversation storage.** `SessionStore`, `SQLiteSessionStore`, and `CustomStorage` persist root history and automatic Python tool results. This initial profile excludes native tools, Environments, children, planning tools, generated-code execution, manual tools, and portable checkpoints. `SQLiteSessionStore` requires one host and a local POSIX filesystem. title: openai/openai-agents-python v0.24.0-alpha.6 — Agents SDK v0.24.0-alpha.6
body:
# Install the preview

Use standard CPython 3.10–3.14 in a virtual environment. These wheels include the native runtime; no Rust toolchain or source build is needed. This preview is distributed through GitHub Releases, not PyPI.

Run the command for your platform:

**Linux x86_64 (glibc 2.39 or newer)**

```sh
python -m pip install "https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/releases/download/v0.24.0-alpha.6/openai_agents-0.24.0a6-cp310-abi3-manylinux_2_39_x86_64.whl"
```

**macOS 11 or newer on Apple Silicon**

```sh
python -m pip install "https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/releases/download/v0.24.0-alpha.6/openai_agents-0.24.0a6-cp310-abi3-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl"
```

**Windows x64**

```powershell
python -m pip install "https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python/releases/download/v0.24.0-alpha.6/openai_agents-0.24.0a6-cp310-abi3-win_amd64.whl"
```

Wheels are not provided for Intel Macs, ARM Linux, ARM Windows, Alpine/musl, PyPy or free-threaded Python. The `cp310-abi3` filenames also support standard CPython 3.11–3.14.

Check the installed version and native module:

```sh
python -c "from importlib.metadata import version; import agents._native; print(version('openai-agents'))"
```

Expect `0.24.0-alpha.6` or its equivalent Python packaging spelling, `0.24.0a6`. `SHA256SUMS` contains checksums for all three wheels.

# Release notes

Changes since `0.24.0-alpha.5`. This preview expands conversation control, state recovery, and tool policies, and includes public API changes.

### Added

- Control submitted work through a captured `Turn`, with `get_result()`, passive `events()`, manual request handling, steering, and cancellation. Queue prompts with `Session.submit(..., if_busy="queue")`, or steer the active Turn with `if_busy="steer"`.
- Add `LocalStorage` to reopen conversations from a local profile, and extend portable `SessionState` capture and recovery. Add idle forks, caller-supplied compaction summaries, and checks for feature support and checkpoint readiness. `LocalStorage` profiles cannot export portable checkpoints.
- Add `NativeOutput` for native strict output and `PromptedOutput` for JSON validated in Python. Optional `max_retries` performs bounded corrections without tools or replaying the task. `LocalStorage` requires `max_retries=0`.
- Handle live manual tool requests and resume supported pending requests from checkpoints. Add experimental external-job recovery through `agents.experimental.deferred` and an optional MCP Tasks adapter.
- Select tools for each submission or model step within the Session's opening permissions. Add native web search, native child checklists, and native goals for local-storage Sessions.

### Highlights

This release graduates execution environments, A2A, evaluation, and core runtime modules from experimental, adds multi-run evaluation and semantic tool argument matching, adds Microsoft Teams and OpenAI Decisions integrations, and makes long multi-turn workflows faster.
* **Execution environments and sandboxes**:
  * `BaseEnvironment`, `LocalEnvironment`, `EnvironmentToolset`, `DaytonaEnvironment`, and `E2BEnvironment` are now stable. ## Python compatibility

This release requires Python 3.11 or later. Python 3.10 support has been removed. Supported and tested Python versions are 3.11 through 3.14.

Includes consolidated Python dependency updates and the bug fixes listed below.

title: MCPHallu: Benchmarking Reasoning, Execution, and Memory Hallucinations in MCP Agents
body:
Large language model agents are increasingly deployed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which allows them to discover and invoke tools across multiple servers at runtime. Existing MCP benchmarks primarily measure task completion; where they diagnose failures, they do so after execution rather than building specific reasoning, execution, and memory failure risks into task construction.
  We introduce MCPHallu, a benchmark for diagnosing hallucination-prone agent failures in MCP environments along three axes: reasoning, execution, and memory. MCPHallu contains 358 tasks across five capability domains and runs on 36 production MCP servers in isolated containers. Each task is designed with a structural trigger that makes one of four subtypes the dominant failure risk: Branch Collapse, Unreachable Goal, Tool Misuse, or Context Forgetting. This design enables subtype-level analysis rather than aggregate task success alone.
  We evaluate fourteen frontier LLM agents from eight vendors on 5{,}012 trajectories. Current MCP agents remain vulnerable to hallucination-inducing tool environments, achieving an average score of 0.642 on a $[0,1]$ scale (higher is better). Failures concentrate on Unreachable Goal tasks, where the average score drops to 0.458 and 23.2\% of runs pass, indicating that agents often continue issuing tool calls or claim successful completion rather than recognizing infeasible goals. Subtype rankings diverge sharply: a model's rank shifts by 6.9 of 13 positions on average across subtypes, and Branch Collapse is uncorrelated with Unreachable Goal across models ($r = -0.12$). MCPHallu is released at https://github.com/J1zz/mcp_hallu.

title: Open-source MCP server that lets LLM agents drive, walk and fly in 3D games in the background (demo reel)
body: I built this so agents could test game mods by actually playing the games, without needing the game in focus or taking over the PC. It's a stdio MCP server, so it works with Claude Code, Codex or any MCP client. A DLL inside the game process handles input and capture, so the game runs unfocused and several games can run at once, each with its own agent. What's in it: navigation to a waypoint on foot, by car, helicopter, boat or horse; a profile/plugin system for per-game details (minimap position, turn rate, marker colours), so a new game is a profile instead of code; aiming; menu and prompt reading (OCR and template matching); and tools for strategy, card and city-builder games. It has a lot of other uses too: mod development, running simulations, repetitive tasks, AI co-op so you can play co-op with an LLM offline, playtesting, and porting old games to get them running on Windows 10/11. Claude Code created and planned the project and wrote much of the code, Claude agents do most of the development and testing, and Codex contributed some of the code. title: Launch HN: Momentic (YC W24) – Agents that catch bugs by using your app
body:
Hey HN, we’re Wei-Wei and Jeff. We’re building Momentic, QA agents that autonomously plan, explore, and bug-bash controls and user flows in your web, iOS, Android, and (soon) desktop apps to catch bugs.

Here’s a demo: https://youtu.be/BFsM-Se1Fh8

We’re both software engineers that spent our careers on dev tooling and infra across companies like Robinhood, Retool, WeWork, and Qualtrics. Testing was always a pain in the ass (esp Playwright and Selenium), so we built agents to do it for us.

Modern day software has a ton of bugs and the change failure rate is only growing faster as coding agent adoption scales. LLMs are really good at generating code, but reinforce their own assumptions, write a ton of useless tests, and are bad at visual understanding. On DeepSWE v1.1, Sonnet 5.5 hit 66.2% pass rate when banned from writing tests, versus 65.3% when allowed.

OSS end-to-end testing frameworks like Playwright, Selenium, or Maestro force you to hardcode implementation details like XPath, text, or aria-* attributes in your tests. Even with agents, these take a nontrivial amount of time and tokens to build and maintain.

In 2023, we saw Nat Friedman drive a browser with GPT-3 via natbot. We were inspired to use this technology to automate the most painful and tedious parts of software engineering: testing. We started with using LLMs to generate and maintain Playwright, but quickly realized that those primitives were fundamentally misaligned with the agentic SDLC. We think the future of QA is agents testing themselves, not writing scripts.

Mo is a custom agent harness for catching bugs that builds on the past 3 years of Momentic and millions of test traces from complex, real-world applications. Mo is built for recall: it finds the most real bugs, though Codex is a bit more precise at 86% vs 84%. The tradeoff is cost: Mo costs $2.67 per bug vs $0.80 for Codex, less than Claude Code and Devin.

- Self-organizing agent graph. Mo builds a directed acyclic graph (DAG) as it explores. Large product areas automatically fork into parallel sub-agents, each with their own browser or device for concurrent execution.

- Specialized agents for domain specific tasks. Planner agents reason over screenshots and video while dedicated locator agents inspect page structure to resolve plain-English interaction targets. Others include image analysis, video understanding, audio generation, and more.

- Parallel agents coordinate through cooperative resource leases. Agents can announce that they’re “using” or “modifying” overlapping resources or fixtures. Multiple “using” claims can coexist, but only a single “modifying” claim can be active on any particular one.

- Scaled infrastructure. Mo ships with a tunnel that lets users expose private sites and local apps to our hosted agents and infra. A single bug bash can spin up 100s of concurrent browsers and devices.

We benchmarked Mo against coding agents on 4 popular open-source apps: Gitea (58.8k stars), Metabase, Twenty (YC), and Saleor, with 1,396 human-labeled bugs. Each agent got the same brief, a fresh E2B sandbox, and no access to source code. Codex and Claude Code used hosted Browserbase browsers, while Devin used its built-in browser. For evaluators, we implemented LLM as a judge (GPT-6.1 Sol) with a human reviewer.

Results from a time-boxed 60-minute run:

- Mo: 269 bugs, 19.3% recall, 84% precision, $2.67 per bug

- Codex (GPT-6.1 Sol + Playwright MCP): 86 bugs, 6.2% recall, 86% precision, $0.80 per bug

- Claude Code (Opus 5.5 + Playwright MCP): 59 bugs, 4.2% recall, 80% precision, $4.09 per bug

- Devin: 27 bugs, 1.9% recall, 84% precision, $3.89 per bug

Mo finds more bugs the more time it has. From 30 to 60 minutes, it went from 177 to 269 bugs (+52%), while Codex gained only 16%.

Results: https://momentic.ai/qa-bench

Write-up: https://momentic.ai/blog/qa-bench

Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/momentic/qa-bench

Harness: https://github.com/momentic-ai/qa-bench

We just shipped PR testing for Vercel and Cloudflare deploy previews and we’re giving every new signup $250 in Mo spend. Paid plans have higher infra capacity and included usage along with options to top up.

We’d love for you to try it out and give us feedback. Feel free to comment here, we’ll be around all day!

title: AttnSR: Attention Step Reward for Long-Horizon Agentic RL
body: Long-horizon LLM agents make multi-step decisions, yet outcome-reward-only reinforcement learning provides little direct supervision for individual steps. We introduce AttnSR, a step-level reward augmentation method that derives reward allocations from policy attention extracted during training replay, without a separately trained reward model or additional rollouts. AttnSR traces backward through the policy model attention graph to estimate the relevance of earlier steps to the final response. The terminal step, measured relative to a running baseline, determines whether these rewards reinforce or penalize the selected steps. In a controlled Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct study, AttnSR consistently outperforms the PPO baseline across all evaluated checkpoints on ALFWorld, raising final held-out success from 91.2% to 97.1%. The ablation experiment shows that the benefit depends on how intermediate rewards are assigned, rather than simple accumulation of step rewards over time. AttnSR also improves ScienceWorld at every checkpoint while cutting environment interactions by 29.9%. These results support policy attention as a practical prior for step-level reward allocation in long-horizon agentic RL. Code is available at https://github.com/fairyshine/AttnSR .
author: Mengsong Wu, Tianchen Zhou, Zhaochen Su, Zhenhua Liu, Zhe Cui

title: Autonomous agents for electricity-system planning
body: Planning electricity systems requires repeated decisions that connect regional resources, investment, operation and network constraints. Here we present an autonomous planning framework that carries prepared regional scenarios through proposal, numerical evaluation, feedback interpretation, redesign and final plan selection. Agents propose investment bounds, storage operating conditions and feeder interventions, interpret numerical feedback, and decide how to revise designs and when to stop. The framework automatically executes annual investment-and-dispatch optimization and representative-feeder verification, applies fixed acceptance criteria and retains the lowest-cost accepted candidate. We evaluate forty carbon-constrained trajectories across ten system-year scenarios in five electricity systems and four countries, using two model deployments and single- and multi-agent architectures. All forty retain candidates satisfying the implemented physical and fixed annual operational carbon-budget checks. Twenty-eight of forty matched reference designs exceed the new scenario ceilings. A separate archive of ninety-six trajectories under a common 1,000 Mt annual ceiling provides matched references and broader regional coverage. The results demonstrate autonomous planning under explicit emissions constraints using public regional data and published institutional demand outlooks.

title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
body: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

title: Beyond Idle Compliance: The Claim–State Gap in Long-Horizon LLM Agents
body: An LLM agent may continue acting without progress, announce completion without a verified effect, produce a technically successful but unauthorized outcome, mistake locally completed subtasks for global closure, or preserve a success report after its evidentiary basis expires. These are distinct failure conditions even when fluent narrative, legitimate tool responses, and apparently successful component actions coexist. This conceptual paper develops an axiomatic claim–state account derived from the separation of operational regimes: intention, invocation, effect, independent observation, admissibility, authority, composition, and time. It formalizes a three-valued judgment of completion claims, proves bounded non-entailment and indistinguishability propositions, and derives five central archetypes—Loop of Death, Delusion of Done, Forbidden Success, Fractured Done, and Zombie Success—within a broader candidate taxonomy. Each archetype is assigned a failure condition, evidence discriminator, negative control, and defeater. A prospective research protocol specifies independent state oracles, evidence-matched conventional baselines, explicit abstention, temporal adjudication, and preregistered tests of prospective prediction. The manuscript reports no new LLM experiment and does not claim empirical prevalence, causal superiority, or an ontologically distinct Large Language Field. Its contribution is a falsifiable boundary-based research program for separating successful execution, warranted reporting, and legitimate closure across long-horizon agent trajectories.

title: MemoryDojo: Benchmarking Poisoning Through LLM Agent Memory
body: LLM agents benefit from using memory systems to improve performance on long-horizon, multi-session tasks. However, memory introduces a critical attack surface. Malicious instructions encountered in one session may be stored and propagated through memory before being retrieved and acted upon in later sessions. Because memory systems differ in how they process and retrieve information, the downstream effects of poisoning can vary significantly across systems. To quantify the effects of poisoning across different memory architectures, we introduce MemoryDojo, a benchmark for tracing the lifecycle of poisoned information through agent memory and measuring its influence on subsequent agent behavior. MemoryDojo is easily extensible, consists of 155 multi-session long-horizon trajectories covering four domains, and supports five different memory systems. Through our evaluation, we find that all memory systems are susceptible to memory poisoning, with substantial variation in downstream effects. We further propose a memory-aware poison optimization process that increases the poisoning efficacy, highlighting differences between memory architectures. We hope that MemoryDojo will support research on understanding and mitigating agentic memory risks.

title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
body: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which large language model agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 1.4x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.
author: Sergey Shirobokov, Ben Jaderberg, Katerina Hristova, George Tsoukalas, Johannes Bausch
